summary: Specifies what is needed to run an IPv6 mesh over Bluetooth Low Energy links using the Internet Protocol Support Profile. RFC 7668 covered only star topologies, while newer Bluetooth specifications allow extended topologies. It does not choose a routing protocol for the mesh. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Small Bluetooth gadgets used to talk only to one hub. Now they can pass messages along each other, like kids passing notes down a row.

questions: ipv6 over bluetooth low energy mesh
ipv6 mesh over bluetooth low energy
what mtu does ipv6 use over bluetooth le
subtitle: How IPv6 packets hop from device to device across a mesh of Bluetooth Low Energy links.

tldr.problem: RFC 7668 put IPv6 on Bluetooth LE for star networks only, but newer Bluetooth versions allow extended topologies, and the star-specific rules would fail in a mesh.
tldr.mechanism: Devices connect with the Bluetooth Internet Protocol Support Profile (IPSP), form one multilink subnet with route-over forwarding, and reuse 6LoWPAN neighbor discovery and RFC 6282 header compression with mesh-aware rules.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track document that makes IPv6 mesh over Bluetooth LE possible, but it deliberately leaves the routing protocol unspecified.

today: RFC 9159 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2021, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on RFC 7668 and leaves routing to other specifications.

sections.title: Why a Mesh Needs New Rules
sections.content:
Bluetooth Low Energy (Bluetooth LE) is a low-power wireless technology for short-range control and monitoring. RFC 7668 described IPv6 over Bluetooth LE, but it was built for star networks, the only shape Bluetooth 4.0 supported. The RFC says that functionality would fail to enable an IPv6 mesh.

This document specifies the mechanisms needed for an IPv6 mesh over Bluetooth LE links. It explicitly does not choose the routing protocol that the mesh uses.
sections.eli5: A hub-and-spoke setup is like a teacher talking to each kid. A mesh is kids passing notes to each other, and that needs new rules.

sections.title: Bluetooth LE Roles and the IPSP
sections.content:
Bluetooth LE defines a central role and a peripheral role. Bluetooth 4.1 let a peripheral connect to more than one central at once, which allows topologies beyond the star. A device may also be a central on some connections and a peripheral on others.

The Internet Protocol Support Profile (IPSP) lets IP-enabled devices find each other and set up a link-layer connection that carries IPv6 packets. It defines a Node role for devices that consume or originate IPv6 packets and a Router role for devices that can route them. Forwarding devices in the mesh have to implement both roles, while simpler leaf-only nodes can implement only the Node role.

Two nodes are neighbors if a link-layer connection exists between them, set up using IPSP.
sections.eli5: Some devices only send and receive their own notes. Others also pass notes along. A device can do both jobs if it needs to.

sections.title: Protocol Stack and MTU
sections.content:
The stack looks like the one in RFC 7668 with two differences. The adaptation layer below IPv6 is now adapted for mesh links, and the stack includes IPv6 routing functionality. A device in the IPSP Node role runs one Internet Protocol Support Service (IPSS) on top of GATT.

Bluetooth 4.2 defines a default Bluetooth LE MTU of 251 bytes. After the 4-byte L2CAP header, 247 bytes remain for the layer above. IPSP negotiates a connection offering an MTU of 1280 octets or higher for IPv6, and this specification sets the MTU for IPv6 mesh over Bluetooth LE links at 1280 octets.

As in RFC 7668, 6LoWPAN fragmentation is not used. The fragmentation and reassembly provided by L2CAP is used instead.
sections.eli5: Big messages get cut into smaller pieces by the Bluetooth layer itself and glued back together at the other end, so the IPv6 layer does not need to do it.

sections.title: One Subnet, Route-Over Forwarding
sections.content:
The RFC chooses a multilink subnet model: the point-to-point links between a central and its peripherals are treated as one subnet, not as many separate subnets. Running a subnet per link and routing between them is judged excessive for constrained IoT nodes. A single global unicast prefix is used on the whole subnet. With this model, routers have to track multicast state and forward multicast in a loop-free way.

Three node types come from RFC 6775: the 6LoWPAN Node (6LN), the 6LoWPAN Router (6LR) and the 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR). One or more 6LBRs connect the mesh to the Internet, and 6LNs reach the network through a 6LR or 6LBR.

IPv6 mesh over Bluetooth LE links MUST follow a route-over approach, meaning packets are routed at the IP layer. The routing protocol itself is not specified.
sections.eli5: The whole mesh shares one street name, and some devices act as crossroads that point messages the right way. The RFC does not say which map they must use.

sections.title: Addresses and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
Addresses are configured as in Section 3.2.2 of RFC 7668. Multihop duplicate address detection from RFC 6775, as updated by RFC 8505, or a substitute mechanism, MAY be supported.

Route-over neighbor discovery from RFC 6775 and RFC 8505 MUST be supported. A 6LN MUST register its non-link-local addresses with its routers using a Neighbor Solicitation carrying the Extended Address Registration Option (EARO). The option includes a Registration Ownership Verifier (ROVR), which by default is the 48-bit Bluetooth device address converted to 64-bit Modified EUI-64 format. A cryptographic ID from RFC 8928 MAY be used instead. A link-local address only needs to be unique between the two nodes using it.

Routers SHALL NOT use multicast Neighbor Solicitations to discover other routers' link-layer addresses. A 6LR starts out using only the IPSP Node role. Once it has a connection to a router and has received a Router Advertisement, it configures its address, becomes a router and runs the IPSP Router role. A 6LBR uses both IPSP roles at all times.
sections.eli5: A new device has to tell its neighbor what name it wants and prove it is the one who owns that name. A helper device only starts passing notes after it has joined a working network.

sections.title: Header Compression and Multicast
sections.content:
Header compression per RFC 6282 is REQUIRED, and all headers MUST be compressed using its formats. The 6LBR MAY include a 6LoWPAN Context Option (6CO) for each prefix it advertises. The star-specific optimizations of RFC 7668 cannot be generalized to a mesh, but a subset still applies to link-local traffic, the first hop from a 6LN and the last hop toward a 6LN. Other traffic MAY use context-based compression.

A sender MUST fully elide the source interface identifier when the source is its own link-local address based on its Bluetooth device address, and the destination when it is the neighbor's link-local address. A 6LN's latest registered address can be fully elided too. An older registered address can carry its last 16 bits inline if the first 48 bits of the identifier match the latest one, and otherwise carries all 64 bits.

The Bluetooth LE Link Layer does not support multicast, so a node replicates multicast packets and unicasts them on each link, which may be costly for battery-powered nodes. A router MUST track neighboring multicast listeners and MUST NOT forward multicast to neighbors that have not registered as listeners.
sections.eli5: Because everyone already knows some of the address from context, devices can leave parts out to make messages shorter. Group messages are sent one by one to each neighbor.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7668 apply. A mesh needs a routing protocol, and routing can create extra opportunities for attacks. RFC 7416 gives an overview of threats and countermeasures for RPL, and its guidance is useful when RPL is used here and may partly apply to other routing protocols.

A ROVR derived from the Bluetooth device address can be spoofed, so a node that knows a registered-address-to-ROVR mapping could steal an address or impersonate its owner. Address Protected Neighbor Discovery (RFC 8928) protects against such attacks. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If a name tag is easy to copy, someone could pretend to be you. Using a harder-to-fake tag stops that.

sections.title: Joining and Bring-Up Examples
sections.content:
Appendix A walks through a network with one 6LBR, two 6LRs and three 6LNs. The 6LBR starts as an IPSP router. The 6LRs start as IPSP nodes and advertise their presence, the 6LBR connects to each, and after receiving Router Advertisements the 6LRs become routers. The 6LNs then start as IPSP nodes, and the 6LRs connect to them.

Appendix B shows a joining node. It sends a Router Solicitation, the 6LR replies with a Router Advertisement carrying a Prefix Information Option, the 6LN registers its new address with an NS carrying EARO, multihop DAD is performed, and the 6LR answers with an NA.
sections.eli5: New devices say hello, learn the street name, register their house number and wait for the okay before joining in.
